Both integrate changes from one branch into another. The difference is what they do to history.

## `git merge`

Creates a new commit that ties the two branches together. Nothing existing is rewritten.

```
      A---B---C  feature
     /         \
D---E---F---G---H  main   (H = merge commit)
```

- History is a truthful record: you can see the branch existed and when it landed.
- Safe on shared branches — no commit hashes change.
- Cost: lots of merge commits make `git log` noisy and diamond-shaped.

## `git rebase`

Replays your commits on top of the new base, one at a time. Old commits are *discarded* and replaced by new ones with new hashes.

```
before:  A---B---C  feature
        /
   D---E---F---G  main

after:   git rebase main
                    A'--B'--C'  feature
                   /
   D---E---F---G  main
```

- History becomes linear and easy to read/bisect.
- Cost: rewrites history. If someone else pulled those commits, their history and yours diverge.
- Conflicts can resurface once per replayed commit instead of once total.

## Practical rules

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| Updating your local feature branch with latest `main` | `rebase` |
| Cleaning up your own messy WIP commits before a PR | `rebase -i` |
| Landing a feature branch into `main` | `merge` (or squash-merge) |
| Branch is shared / already pushed and others pulled it | `merge` — never rebase |

The golden rule: **don't rebase commits that exist outside your own machine.** If you rebase after pushing, you need `git push --force-with-lease`, and anyone who pulled the old version has to recover manually.

One more distinction people trip on: `git pull` defaults to merge, which sprinkles "Merge branch 'main' of origin/main" commits into your history. `git pull --rebase` (or `git config --global pull.rebase true`) avoids that.

Both integrate one branch's work into another. The difference is what happens to history.

**Setup for the demo above:** `feature` has two commits (A, B) branched off `base`; meanwhile `main` got its own commit (C).

## Merge — preserves history, adds a commit

```
*   14e58db Merge branch 'feature'
|\
| * 88cfdc9 feature: B
| * 9319842 feature: A
* | c2c039f main: C
|/
* c283160 base
```

- Creates a **merge commit** with two parents, tying the branches back together.
- Original commits keep their hashes (`9319842`, `88cfdc9`) — nothing is rewritten.
- The graph records *what actually happened*: work happened in parallel, then converged.
- Non-destructive and safe on shared branches.

## Rebase — rewrites history, replays commits

```
* 0acb931 feature: B
* dca0c36 feature: A
* 4c473f9 main: C
* e89bfea base
```

- Takes your commits, and **replays them one at a time** on top of the new base.
- Note the hashes changed: `9319842` → `dca0c36`. These are *new commits* with the same content, different parents. The originals are orphaned.
- Result is a **linear history** — no merge commit, no fork in the graph.
- `git log` reads as a clean story; `git bisect` and `git log --oneline` are easier to follow.

## The practical rules

| | merge | rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | true, branchy | linear, tidy |
| Commit hashes | preserved | rewritten |
| Conflict resolution | once, in the merge commit | potentially once **per commit** replayed |
| Safe on pushed branches | yes | **no** — needs `--force-with-lease` |

**The golden rule: never rebase commits that others have pulled.** Rewriting shared history means everyone else's clone diverges from yours, and their next `git pull` creates a mess of duplicate commits.

**Common workflow that gets the best of both:**
```bash
git checkout feature
git rebase main      # tidy up your local branch onto latest main
git checkout main
git merge --no-ff feature   # merge commit marks the feature boundary
```
Rebase privately to clean up, merge publicly to integrate.

Also worth knowing: `git rebase -i` (interactive) is the tool for squashing WIP commits, reordering, and rewording before you open a PR — that's arguably rebase's more common day-to-day use than integration.

One caveat on the demo: I resolved no conflicts here since the branches touched different regions. With real conflicts, rebase can stop repeatedly (once per replayed commit) while merge stops once — that's the sharpest practical pain difference, and it's not visible in the output above.

**Identical end result, different history.** Both repos finished with the exact same tree hash `049ae26` — same files, same content. The difference is entirely in the shape of the log.

### Merge

Creates a new commit with two parents, joining the branches:

```
*   d52de67 Merge branch 'feature'
|\
| * 6bc20f1 D: more feature
| * 5ab554b C: feature work
* | eb7dc43 B: main work
|/
* 5509df9 A: base
```

- Existing commits are never modified — `5ab554b` and `6bc20f1` keep their original SHAs.
- History records *when* integration actually happened, and that these commits were developed in parallel.
- Non-destructive and safe on shared branches.
- Cost: the graph accumulates merge bubbles, and `git log` interleaves work from many branches.

### Rebase

Replays your commits on top of the new base, one at a time:

```
* 064a87d D: more feature
* 09e64d7 C: feature work
* e51e200 B: main work
* aa0daff A: base
```

- Commits are **rewritten**, not moved — `5ab554b` → `09e64d7`, `6bc20f1` → `064a87d` in the run above. New SHAs, new parents, same diffs.
- History becomes linear and reads like sequential development, even though it wasn't.
- Conflicts are resolved per-commit, so a long branch can make you fix the same conflict repeatedly (`git rerere` helps).
- Because the old commits are discarded, pushing requires `--force-with-lease`.

### The rule that matters

Don't rebase commits that others have pulled. Rewriting shared history forces everyone else to reconcile diverged branches by hand. The safe split most teams use:

- **Rebase** your own local feature branch onto updated `main` before opening a PR — cleans up "merge main into feature" noise.
- **Merge** the feature into `main` (often `--no-ff`) so the integration point stays recorded.

A middle option: `git pull --rebase` for routine syncing of your own work, which avoids the pointless merge commits that plain `git pull` creates when you and a teammate both pushed.

One caveat on my demo, stated as a limit rather than a claim: it contains no conflicting edits, so it demonstrates the history shapes only — it does not exercise the conflict-resolution differences described above.

Both integrate changes from one branch into another; they differ in what history they leave behind.

## `git merge`

Creates a new commit that ties two histories together. Nothing existing is rewritten.

```
      A---B---C  feature
     /         \
D---E---F---G---M  main
```

- History is preserved exactly as it happened, including the fact that work happened in parallel.
- Safe on shared branches — commit hashes never change.
- Cost: lots of merge commits, and `git log` on a busy repo becomes a braid.
- Conflicts are resolved **once**, in the merge commit.

## `git rebase`

Replays your commits on top of a new base, creating *new commits* with new hashes. The old ones become unreachable.

```
git checkout feature
git rebase main

                  A'--B'--C'  feature
                 /
D---E---F---G  main
```

- Linear history — `git log` reads like a story instead of a graph.
- Cost: history is a fiction. It looks like you wrote the feature on top of `G`, which you didn't.
- Conflicts can surface **per replayed commit**, so a long branch may make you resolve the same conflict repeatedly (`git rerere` helps).
- `--force-with-lease` is required to push afterward.

## The rule that matters

**Never rebase commits that others have pulled.** Rewriting shared history forces everyone else to reconcile a branch whose commits vanished. Rebase your own unpushed/unshared work freely; merge when the branch is public.

## Practical workflow most teams land on

```bash
# keep your feature branch current — rebase (yours, unshared)
git checkout feature
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main

# integrate into main — merge, with a commit marking the feature
git checkout main
git merge --no-ff feature
```

That gives you a clean, linear feature branch *and* a main branch where each feature is one identifiable merge point.

## Related tools

- `git merge --squash` — collapse a branch into a single commit on the target, no merge commit.
- `git rebase -i` — reorder, squash, reword, or drop commits before sharing. (Not available in this environment, but standard elsewhere.)
- `git pull --rebase` — avoids the "Merge branch 'main' into 'main'" noise commits from routine pulls. Worth setting globally: `git config --global pull.rebase true`.

## Quick decision table

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| Updating your local feature branch from main | rebase |
| Landing a finished feature into main | merge (`--no-ff`) |
| Branch already pushed and someone else pulled it | merge |
| Cleaning up messy WIP commits before a PR | interactive rebase |
| You want an auditable record of what actually happened | merge |

```

     /
A---B---C  main
```

Creates a new **merge commit** `M` with two parents:

```
      D---E---M  feature
     /       /
A---B---C----  main
```

- Existing commits are never rewritten — `D` and `E` keep their hashes.
- History records that a branch existed and when it was integrated.

Replays your commits on top of `main`'s tip as **new** commits:

```

A---B---C----  main
```

## Which to use

| Situation | Choice |
|---|---|
| Updating your local feature branch with upstream changes | `rebase` — keeps your work on top, avoids noise merges |
| Branch already pushed and someone else may have it | `merge` — rebasing rewrites history others depend on |
| Landing a finished feature into `main` | Team convention; `merge --no-ff` preserves branch context, `rebase` + fast-forward keeps `main` linear |
| You want an accurate record of what actually happened | `merge` |
| You want a readable, bisect-friendly straight line | `rebase` |

## The one rule that matters

**Don't rebase commits that exist outside your machine.** Rebasing changes hashes, so anyone who pulled the old commits gets a divergent history and a painful reconciliation. If you must, use `git push --force-with-lease` (not plain `--force`) and tell your collaborators.

- `git pull --rebase` — rebases your local commits on top of the fetched branch instead of making a merge commit. Set it as default with `git config --global pull.rebase true`.

## The cache key is a chain, not a set

Docker doesn't cache instructions individually. Each layer's cache key is a hash of:

1. **The parent layer's ID**, plus
2. The instruction text itself, plus
3. For `COPY`/`ADD`, a checksum of the files being copied

Point 1 is the whole answer. Because the parent's ID feeds into the child's key, an instruction's cache identity depends on *everything before it*. Move a line, and it lands on a different parent → different key → miss. That miss produces a new layer ID → the next instruction's parent changed → miss. It cascades to the end of the stage.

Lookup is also a linear walk from the base image that stops at the first miss. There's no "skip ahead and re-find the cache later."

```dockerfile
# Build A                    # Build B (last two swapped)
RUN apt-get install -y curl  RUN apt-get install -y curl
COPY package.json .          RUN npm config set foo bar   ← new parent, miss
RUN npm config set foo bar   COPY package.json .          ← identical text, still miss
```

`COPY package.json .` is byte-identical in both and the file is unchanged — but its parent differs, so it misses anyway.

## The second mechanism: `COPY` sees different content

Reordering can also change *what* a `COPY` captures. `COPY . .` before vs. after a `RUN` that generates files copies a different tree, so the checksum in point 3 changes for real.

## Things that look like reordering but aren't

- `ARG`/`ENV` lines participate in the key, and an `ARG` also invalidates every instruction after it that references it.
- BuildKit is more forgiving *across* stages — independent stages have independent chains, and identical steps get deduped — but within one stage the parent-chaining rule is unchanged.
- `--mount=type=cache` (BuildKit) survives layer invalidation. It's why a busted `RUN npm ci` layer can still finish fast: the layer re-runs, but the package cache persists.

## The practical rule

Order instructions **least-frequently-changing first**. The canonical shape:

```dockerfile
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./   # changes rarely
RUN npm ci                               # expensive, stays cached
COPY . .                                 # changes every commit
RUN npm run build
```

Inverting those last two — `COPY . .` before `RUN npm ci` — means every source edit re-runs the install. That's the same failure as reordering, just made permanent.

## The mechanism

The build cache is a **chain**, not a set. Each instruction produces a layer whose cache key is a hash of roughly:

```
parent_layer_digest + the instruction string (+ content checksum, for COPY/ADD)
```

The parent digest is in the key. That's the whole answer: an instruction's identity in the cache depends on everything above it. Change *anything* at line N — including just moving a line — and every layer from N down gets a new parent, hence a new key, hence a miss. The instructions below are byte-identical and still miss, because "identical instruction, different parent" is a different layer.

So swapping two completely independent `RUN` lines busts everything from the earlier of the two positions onward, even though nothing semantically changed.

## The version that actually bites people

```dockerfile
COPY . .
RUN npm ci          # ← rebuilt on every source edit
```

vs.

```dockerfile
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci          # ← only rebuilt when the manifests change
COPY . .
```

For `COPY`/`ADD`, the key also folds in a checksum of the copied files' contents and metadata (mode, ownership — not mtime, under BuildKit). Copying the whole tree early means any touched source file changes that layer's key, and the expensive install below it inherits the miss. Hence the standard ordering rule: **least-frequently-changing instructions first, most-volatile last.**

## Things that count as "a change" and often surprise

- `ENV` / `ARG` / `LABEL` lines — they're instructions, so editing or reordering them invalidates downstream even if nothing consumes them. An `ARG` whose value is *used* below also changes the expanded `RUN` string.
- `RUN` command text — whitespace, flag order, a reworded `&&` chain. It's a string compare, not semantic.
- Comments and blank lines are stripped by the parser and don't affect keys.
- Reordering *within* a multi-stage stage doesn't touch other stages — each stage has its own chain — but it does invalidate anything that `COPY --from`s the changed output.

## The escape hatch

The chained-parent rule is what cache mounts sidestep:

```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci
```

The layer still misses on reorder, but the mount persists across builds, so the re-run is a warm-cache install instead of a cold download. Same idea for `~/.cargo`, `/root/.cache/pip`, apt lists.

**PUT** — that's exactly the case it's designed for.

```
PUT /widgets/my-chosen-id
```

The URI is known before the request, so the request targets it directly. That makes the call idempotent: retry after a timeout and you get the same resource, not a duplicate. With `POST /widgets` carrying the ID in the body, a retried request that the server actually processed the first time either creates a second resource or 409s, and the client can't tell which happened.

Details worth getting right:

- **PUT is create-or-replace.** If you want create-only, add `If-None-Match: *` — the server returns `412 Precondition Failed` if the ID is taken. Without it, a PUT to an existing ID overwrites.
- **Status codes:** `201 Created` with a `Location` header when it creates, `200`/`204` when it replaces.
- **Full representation.** PUT bodies are the complete resource. Partial updates are PATCH.

Merge preserves history; rebase rewrites it.

`git merge main` creates a merge commit joining two branches — your commits keep their original hashes and parents, and the graph shows the branch actually existed.

`git rebase main` replays your commits one at a time onto the tip of main — new hashes, linear history, no merge commit, and it looks like you started from main all along.

Practical rule: rebase your own unpushed local branch to keep history clean, merge anything already shared. Rebasing pushed commits changes hashes others have, forcing `--force-with-lease` and breaking their clones.

Conflicts differ too: merge resolves once; rebase can make you resolve the same conflict per replayed commit (`git rerere` or `--continue` per step).

- Merge conflicts resolve once; rebase can hit conflicts per replayed commit.
- Merge keeps the true record of when work diverged; rebase gives a clean, bisect-friendly log.

- **Multiprocessing** — separate processes, separate GILs, real CPU parallelism.
- **C extensions** — NumPy, SciPy, and friends release the GIL during heavy computation; BLAS threads run in parallel.
